source.title: Theory of overparametrization in quantum neural networks
source.authors: Martín Larocca; Nathan Ju; Diego García-Martín; Patrick J. Coles; M. Cerezo

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary information are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports gradient-based optimization results for quantum neural networks, extending overparameterization findings to a different model setting and to eigensolver, compilation, and autoencoding tasks. It does not test the listed classical-network claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own QNN optimization and rank results. These use quantum circuits and task-specific losses, not CIFAR classification error; cited classical overparameterization results are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests optimization in parametrized quantum circuits. None of V1–V6 names this kind of system: increasing quantum-circuit depth and parameter count does not test CIFAR classification, ReLU teacher-student width, classical depth degradation, initialization, stability-threshold dynamics, or batch normalization. Classical overparameterization results provide background.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors define quantum overparameterization through saturation of achievable QFIM ranks and prove DLA-based bounds on QFIM rank, capacity, and Hessian rank at optima. Their simulations associate increasing parameter count with improved convergence, interpreted as a more favorable landscape with fewer false traps. This should not be strengthened into a general proof that all spurious minima disappear. Hardware-efficient ansatzes may require exponentially many parameters, whereas suitable polynomial-DLA ansatzes offer more scalable possibilities.
record.recipe_differences: Quantum circuits and quantum task losses are studied; the experiments use Adam with full state-vector simulations and no sampling noise, rather than classical classification training.
record.method_sensitivity: Task and ansatz affect the reported threshold and scaling: the Hamiltonian variational ansatz has polynomially scaling DLA dimensions in the stated VQE setting, whereas the hardware-efficient ansatz has an exponentially growing DLA dimension. Boundary condition also changes the stated DLA scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Across open- and closed-boundary VQE simulations, increasing circuit depth improves convergence; open-boundary success probability approaches one around the relevant DLA dimension.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested Hamiltonian variational quantum circuits, increasing parameter count past a task-dependent threshold improves noiseless Adam optimization.

fits_no_version.finding: Quantum unitary-compilation success increases sharply around a parameter count comparable to the DLA dimension.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested hardware-efficient quantum circuits and Haar-random targets, additional circuit parameters improve compilation success until saturation.

fits_no_version.finding: The overparameterized four-qubit autoencoder converges accurately in few iterations, while its QFIM rank at sampled random points is 30 versus a stated DLA dimension of 256.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this quantum autoencoding setup, rapid optimization can coexist with a state-space rank substantially below the DLA dimension.

record.problems: The simulations are small quantum-circuit problems, not classical benchmark classification. Numerical results are presented largely as plots, with only qualitative threshold descriptions in the text. Optimization uses noiseless full-state-vector simulations without sampling noise.
record.rows_left_out: No results left out. Figure-only per-depth and per-size numerical values were not reconstructed from plots.

untested.parts: All parts: classical convolutional networks, CIFAR training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and size, stopping, and regularization conditions.
All parts: two-layer ReLU teacher-student systems, spurious-minimum frequencies, and one- or two-neuron student-width increments.
All parts: classical plain-network depth degradation, identity shortcuts, longer training, and the specified initialization and normalization exceptions.
All parts: activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, Gaussian versus orthogonal weights, and trainable classical-network depth.
All parts: learning rates relative to the initial stability threshold, transient loss increases, curvature dynamics, edge-of-stability training, and divergence.
All parts: batch-normalization comparisons for training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup training without normalization.

record.verdict_notes: States are assessed against V1–V6, so cannot_determine does not dispute the reported quantum effects. No version-relevant missing results were found in the supplied text. All simulations use noiseless full-state-vector evaluation and Adam.

versions.untested_parts: Classical convolutional networks, CIFAR-10/100 classification error, corrupted or random labels, and the stated size, stopping, and regularization conditions.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and the stated teacher/student width comparisons.
Plain versus residual classical convolutional networks, depth-related classification training error, and the cited initialization or normalization recipes.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation in classical networks, and the cited deep tanh and convolutional training results.
Learning rates around the stability threshold, loss-curvature dynamics, and divergence behavior in the stated classical-network settings.
Batch normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance in the stated classical-network settings, and Fixup results.

rows.subject: Hamiltonian variational ansatz (open boundary conditions)
rows.operation_detail: Adam optimization of the transverse-field Ising VQE loss across circuit depths; success probability is the fraction converging within 10−7 of the true solution.
rows.measure: Success probability / convergence to global optimum
rows.value: At M ∼ dim(gS), success probability rapidly goes to one; small layer counts fail to accurately find the ground state, while large layer counts rapidly converge.
rows.uncertainty: 50 randomly-initialized instances; training-curve shading is standard deviation.
rows.locator: Results, Variational Quantum Eigensolver; Figures 3 and 4(a)
rows.note: The text gives qualitative convergence findings and the threshold relation; the plotted per-size probabilities are not transcribed.
rows.check: The quantum VQE convergence result is accurately summarized but cannot establish any listed version. The relevant comparison is shallower circuits with fewer parameters, rather than an unspecified baseline.

rows.subject: Hamiltonian variational ansatz (closed boundary conditions)
rows.operation_detail: Adam optimization of the transverse-field Ising VQE loss across circuit depths; success probability is the fraction converging within 10−7 of the true solution.
rows.measure: Loss relative to exact ground-state energy and convergence with iteration
rows.value: The paper reports that sufficiently deep circuits rapidly converge to the solution; loss decreases exponentially with each optimization step when layer count is large enough.
rows.uncertainty: 50-run average; shaded regions represent standard deviation.
rows.note: Curve values by qubit count and depth are figure-only and not assigned numerical values.
rows.check: Closed-boundary VQE training curves bear on none of the versions. Figure 3 reports energy error and convergence; the explicitly defined 10^-7 success-probability measurement in Figure 4(a) concerns open boundaries and should not be attributed to this row.

rows.subject: Hardware efficient ansatz
rows.operation_detail: Adam optimization of unitary compilation loss over circuit depths; success is convergence within 10−7 of the global optimum.
rows.measure: Success probability / convergence to global optimum
rows.value: Around dim(gS) parameters are required to consistently find high-quality solutions; convergence probability undergoes a drastic phase transition around dim(gS).
rows.note: The text describes the threshold behavior; plotted values by size and depth are not transcribed.
rows.check: Unitary-compilation convergence concerns quantum circuits, not the systems or measures in V1–V6. The relevant baseline is circuits with fewer layers and parameters.

rows.subject: Hardware efficient ansatz
rows.operation_detail: Adam optimization of the quantum autoencoding loss for circuits with the stated layer counts.

conditions.value: four states drawn from the NTangled dataset

rows.measure: Loss and convergence to global optimum
rows.value: The overparametrized QNN is reported to reach the global optimum accurately in few iterations.
rows.note: The training curves are plotted; the text provides only the qualitative result.
rows.check: Quantum autoencoding tests none of the versions. Attribute rapid accurate convergence to the overparameterized L=35 circuit; L=5 is the comparison condition, and the stated favorable outcome should not be assigned jointly to both.

rows.subject: Hardware efficient ansatz
rows.operation_detail: Measured QFIM rank at random points in the loss landscape.

rows.note: The paper contrasts this with dim(gS) = 256 and notes that this suggests overparametrization may occur with fewer parameters than dim(gS).
rows.check: The reported QFIM rank of 30 is a quantum state-space dimension measurement, not an optimization outcome named by any version. It can remain a descriptive result but cannot receive a version-relative observed state.
